newsitem.title: USA: U.S. beef exports to Japan seen slowly rebounding.
newsitem.headline: U.S. beef exports to Japan seen slowly rebounding.

text.p: U.S. beef exports to Japan may be slowly recovering after dropping sharply over the summer in the wake of a deadly outbreak of food poisoning there that was exacerbated by the "mad cow" scare in Europe.
"We have heard from some of our exporters that we have bottomed out and turned the corner," said Ron Willis, a beef director at the Denver-based U.S. Meat Export Federation.
However, a recent E.coli bacterial outbreak that sickened 17 people in Japan, including 15 children, could a cause a new slowdown in meat consumption there, Willis said.
The source of the latest outbreak, as well as previous ones that killed 11 people and made more than 9,500 ill in Japan, has not been positively identified.
U.S. meat packing giant IBP Inc. reported a drop in beef exports to the Far East because of the publicity surrounding the illneses.
"I think the worst is behind us," said Bob Price, livestock analyst with Cargill Investor Services. "I think they (Japanese) are showing better interest for cuts that have to be cooked."
Japan is the leading U.S. export market for beef and pork.

The "mad cow" scare upset British and other European beef exports after researchers early this year said eating beef from cows infected with Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), also called mad cow disease, could possibly cause a degenerative brain disorder in humans.
"What we saw is they (Japanese) basically quit eating meat," Willis said. "We expect August and September exports to be off 20 to 30 percent," vs. a year ago.
Shipments to Japan increased during the first six months of the year, but have fallen off since July.
Beef shipments during the first six months totalled 661 million pounds, up from 439 million pounds a year ago, and pork shipments totalled 340 million pounds, up from 188 million pounds.

Japan's Finance Ministry reported that total beef imports were down 29.5 percent in August and pork imports down 46.5 percent from year-earlier levels. Shipments from the United States were down 34 percent for beef and 23 percent for pork for the period.
Pork exports were not as severely hurt because pork typically is well cooked, lessening the chance of E. coli poisoning.
The drop in exports has been good news for U.S. consumers. Prices for some beef cuts have dropped because beef that would normally be exported was diverted to U.S. supermarkets.

"That's one reason we have lower prices," said Kevin Bost, a market analyst for Topco Associates Inc. Topco is a supplier of meat and other foods to supermarkets nationwide, and Bost estimated prices for some beef cuts are down 5 percent to 10 percent from a year ago.
Wholesale prices for boneless rib roasts averaged $3.60 per pound since mid-August vs. $3.77 a year ago, and beef sirloin prices averaged $2.62 vs. $2.88.
Prices for ground beef, chuck and round cuts were up slightly from a year ago because of an overall decline in U.S. beef production, but these cuts are not normally exported,Bost noted.
